title: Chaos continues for passengers stranded after U.S. airspace closed for hours

image.caption: People wait in line to rebook cancelled flights at Pearson International Airport in Toronto on Friday. (Sandra Ezekwesili/The Canadian Press)

items: November 14Few passengers, short waits at Toronto's Pearson airportHello, I'm Katie Simpson, a senior Washington correspondent with CBC News. Today I’m flying from Toronto's Pearson airport to Washington Dulles airport, as my flight is one of a few that has not yet been cancelled. Inside Pearson's Terminal 1 at the F gate, where many flights headed to the U.S. depart from, it is unusually quiet for a Saturday morning. The security process took less than five minutes, and there was no one waiting in line ahead of me to go through customs.

McCormick says he's worried there isn't robust testing of FAA system upgradesAnya ZoledziowskiU.S. officials blame now-cancelled ground stop on outdated equipment, underfundingU.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the now-cancelled national ground stop order that snarled air traffic on 'outdated equipment' and a lack of Congressional funding in what, at times, sounded like a partisan political rant against Democrats.Following the ground stop, U.S. officials blamed outdated equipment for the failure. But former FAA manager McCormick says that it's tricky to update air traffic control systems all in one go.When speaking with CBC News, McCormick, who famously shut down U.S. airspace on Sept. 11, also said that he's worried the FAA's system upgrades haven't been adequately tested. "The challenge is that trying to upgrade an air traffic control system is like trying to change the tire on a car while the car is still moving," McCormick said. "You can't just shut it down and put a new air traffic control system in its place. You have to keep the old system up and running."According to the former FAA manager, it seems a newer system overloaded an existing system, which led to the damage. That's why he's worried about whether there was robust enough testing prior to the update's integration.The FAA said in a statement it "thoroughly tested" its systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume.But don't panic; McCormick says yesterday's ground stop is a lesson learned."I'm not concerned to the point where I'm not going to fly," he said.-With files from The Associated Press

Former FAA air traffic manager says recovery will take 2 to 3 daysAnya ZoledziowskiGround stop aftermath: Why it will take days to get things back to normalCancelling the FAA ground stop order was just the first step in getting planes moving again. The National asks former FAA manager Michael McCormack to explain why it could take up to 3 days to fully restart air travel after such a major disruption.Former FAA air traffic manager Michael McCormick told CBC News that airlines will need time to sort out their operations — something that will likely take the whole weekend."You have aircraft, air crews, passenger baggage, and they're stuck in locations where they're needed elsewhere," McCormick said. "It takes time and a lot of effort to reschedule all those aircraft and air crews to be where they need to be."Airlines also have to determine which flights to delay and which ones to cancel outright, McCormick said. "Some airlines will choose to delay the flights because they need that aircraft and air crew to get to the destination airport," he said. "Other times they may choose to cancel flights because air crews may run out of their flight time and they won't be able to actually fly the aircraft."

Canadian airlines warn passengers of possible delays, cancellationsAnya ZoledziowskiPeople wait in line to rebook cancelled flights at Pearson International Airport in Toronto on Friday. (Sandra Ezekwesili/The Canadian Press)As Canadian airlines recover from yesterday's nationwide ground stop in the U.S., they're warning passengers that recovery will take some time."Schedules may continue to be impacted as operations recover," Air Canada wrote in a statement. "If your flight is impacted or if there are any changes to your itinerary, we'll notify you via email and text message."Air Canada advised passengers to monitor their flight status,WestJet meanwhile said that travellers flying to and from the U.S., Mexico or Caribbean between Friday and Sunday can make a one-time change or cancellation without penalty. But the airline warned that call centre wait times will be longer than usual.

Travellers brace for chaotic weekend after U.S. airspace shutdownAnya ZoledziowskiStranded passengers wait at Cancun International Airport after aircraft at Mexican airports with U.S.-bound flights were asked to stay on the ground on Friday. (Paola Chiomante/Reuters)This weekend will continue to be chaotic for travellers in the U.S. — and beyond. Yesterday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) suffered a communications issue in the afternoon — caused by aging and overloaded air traffic control systems, according to the White House — that catapulted the country into a nationwide airport shutdown lasting more than four hours. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed, including in Canada, creating chaos and uncertainty for airlines and travellers. It's only the third time the FAA has grounded flights nationwide in 25 years. The first lasted two days following the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. And on Jan 11, 2023, the FAA paused domestic departures for some 90 minutes, also because of a communications issue.It will likely take days for U.S. flight to return to normal.
